turns.doctor_question: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, yeah, thank you for fitting me in. So, I guess the main reason I’m here—and honestly, I’ve been wrestling with whether or not to even make this appointment for weeks now—is that work has just become this... this impossible hurdle. 

I’m a medical services manager, so I oversee operations for a few different clinics, and, you know, I'm usually great at putting out fires and dealing with people face-to-face. But anything that takes real, sitting-down brain work... it just feels like I physically hit a brick wall. For example, I have these monthly reports—compliance, staffing metrics, budget variances, that kind of thing—and right now we’re also trying to plan this massive multi-site health event for the community. It’s a huge deal, lots of moving parts, coordinating between different facilities. 

But when I sit down at my desk, close the door, and try to actually map it out or dig into the data, my brain just completely stops. I keep putting it off. I’ll find a million other minor things to do instead, like reorganizing my email folders or walking down to check on the front desk, even though I know exactly how much these big projects matter. The directors are counting on me for that multi-site event, the board needs those monthly reports, and I *know* it matters, I really do. But sitting down and forcing myself to do that heavy mental lifting... I just avoid it. I avoid it until the absolute last possible second, and it's really starting to catch up with me. I just sit there staring at the screen, and I don't know, it's incredibly frustrating because I know I have the capability to do it, I have my degree, I've been in healthcare management for years, but lately I just... I can't get over that wall.

symptom_reasoning.S006: The patient explicitly describes avoiding and putting off tasks that require 'heavy mental lifting' or 'sitting-down brain work,' such as writing reports and planning events.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back, did you experience similar difficulties with focus and getting through tedious tasks when you were younger, such as during your school years?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, wow, yeah. It’s funny you ask that because, honestly, I haven't thought about it in a long time, but... yes. Absolutely. I mean, going all the way back to elementary school, it was the exact same story. I remember my parents coming home from parent-teacher conferences—it didn't even matter which grade, third, fourth, fifth, it was always the exact same conversation. 

The teachers would always sit them down and say, you know, that I was a really bright kid, that I had all this potential and understood the material when I actually engaged with it, but that I was just constantly daydreaming. I’d just be staring out the window, completely in my own little world while everyone else was focused on the chalkboard. And the paperwork... God, the worksheets. It was like my desk and my backpack were just these black holes. They’d hand out a math worksheet or a spelling packet, and I swear to you, within five minutes it was just gone. Crumpled up, lost, shoved inside a textbook somewhere. 

And the homework was a whole other nightmare. Half the time I’d actually do the work, but then I’d just completely forget to turn it in. It would just sit there in my folder. The only reason I ever passed those early grades was because of my mother. Bless her, she worked full time too, but every single night, without fail, she had to physically sit me down at the kitchen table, take my backpack, and dump the entire thing out. She would go through every single crumpled piece of paper, every folder, just to make sure my homework was done and actually packed in a way that I might remember to hand it to the teacher the next morning. If she didn't check my backpack every night, nothing would have ever made it back to the classroom. 

So, yeah, looking back, that feeling of just... drifting away when I’m supposed to be doing something tedious, it's exactly like what I’m dealing with now with these budget reports at the clinic. It’s incredibly frustrating to realize that I’m 46 years old and I'm basically still that same nine-year-old kid losing his worksheets, just on a much more expensive scale, you know? It's like my brain just refuses to hold onto the boring details, no matter how hard I try to force it.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient states their brain refuses to hold onto boring details.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes constantly daydreaming and drifting away during tedious tasks.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient mentions failing to follow through by not turning in completed homework.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes their desk and backpack as black holes, requiring their mother to organize their school materials.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient frequently lost worksheets and paperwork within minutes of receiving them.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient was easily distracted, staring out the window and being in their own world during class.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient frequently forgot to turn in their homework.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from difficulties with focus, do you often experience physical restlessness, such as trouble sitting still or a constant need to be on the move?
turns.patient_response:
No, not really. I mean, I don't feel like I have ants in my pants or anything like that. I know some people get really fidgety, bouncing their legs up and down, pacing around the room when they're on a phone call—my brother is actually like that, he can't sit through a whole movie without getting up to get water or check his phone or just stretch his legs. But for me, it's not a physical thing at all. 

I can sit at my desk for hours. That's actually part of the problem. I'll sit there, in my chair, door closed, completely still, just... staring at the monitor. My body is totally fine being parked in one spot. It's my brain that's doing the wandering. It's like my physical body is anchored to the chair, but my mind is a million miles away, thinking about what I need to pick up at the grocery store, or replaying a conversation I had with one of the clinic directors three days ago, or wondering if I need to rotate the tires on my car. 

So, yeah, I wouldn't say I'm physically restless. I don't feel this overwhelming urge to jump up and run a marathon or even just walk down the hall, unless I'm using it as an excuse to avoid the budget spreadsheet, of course. But even then, it's not because my body *needs* to move, it's just because my brain is desperately looking for an escape hatch from the mental effort. It's a very internal, quiet kind of chaos, if that makes sense. Not the jumping-off-the-walls kind. Just... sitting perfectly still while my focus completely evaporates.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient states their focus completely evaporates while sitting still, indicating difficulty sustaining attention.
symptom_reasoning.S006: The patient mentions looking for an excuse to avoid the budget spreadsheet because their brain wants an escape hatch from the mental effort.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes their mind wandering to unrelated thoughts like grocery lists or past conversations while trying to work.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly denies being fidgety or having 'ants in their pants'.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient denies leaving their seat, stating they can sit at their desk for hours and are fine being parked in one spot.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly states, 'I wouldn't say I'm physically restless.'
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient denies feeling an overwhelming urge to be on the move or being the 'jumping-off-the-walls kind'.
